title: ICE Arrests Soar to Nearly 50,000 in July, Highest Monthly Total of Trump Era
excerpt: A strategic shift to lower-profile enforcement across airports, courthouses, and traffic stops drove a 15 percent surge in arrests, backed by billions in new funding and 12,000 new officers.
body:
• ICE recorded 49,571 arrests in July 2026, the highest monthly total of Trump's second term and a 15% jump over June's 43,021
  • More than half of arrests came from four states — Texas, Florida, California, and Georgia — with state and local police playing an expanding enforcement role through 287(g) agreements
  • The surge reflects a strategic shift under DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin toward lower-profile but more widespread enforcement, including arrests at airports, courthouses, and traffic stops

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 49,571 people in July, setting the highest single-month arrest total during President Trump's second term and marking a 15 percent increase over June's already record-breaking figure of 43,021, according to government data released by the Deportation Data Project at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

The July total averages 1,599 apprehensions per day and represents a 70 percent increase from 29,241 arrests in February, when enforcement dipped following the fatal shooting of two American citizens during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis. The figures, obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit and analyzed by The Associated Press, underscore how the administration's mass deportation agenda has accelerated despite a deliberate shift away from the high-profile tactics that drew public backlash earlier in the year.

A Quieter but Broader Crackdown

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who replaced Kristi Noem in March, pledged during his confirmation hearing to keep ICE out of the headlines while still delivering on the administration's deportation goals. Under Noem, enforcement operations were characterized by social media videos of officers bursting from vans and rappelling from helicopters onto apartment rooftops in cities like Chicago, Los Angeles, and Minneapolis.

https://x.com/pslnational/status/2093053288241623073

"They changed the tactics and are, if anything, being more effective."

— Mark Krikorian, Center for Immigration Studies

Graeme Blair, co-director of the Deportation Data Project, told NPR the numbers reflect a broadening of arrest methods. "What we're seeing is an expansion in all of the different ways that ICE is detaining people," Blair said. "They're arresting people at airports, at ICE check-ins, at immigration courthouses and this is the result of that."

State Partnerships Fuel the Surge

More than half of July's arrests came from four states: Texas, Florida, California, and Georgia. Texas and Florida alone accounted for nearly 20,000 arrests, according to the AP analysis.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=gIpV3oBHo_U

Three of the four top states participate in the federal 287(g) program, which allows state and local law enforcement to carry out immigration enforcement duties under ICE direction. Florida leads the nation, with all 67 counties having signed cooperation agreements with ICE, according to the Florida Sheriffs Association.

The numbers were also driven by the initial wave of arrests of Haitian immigrants whose Temporary Protected Status was revoked in July after the Supreme Court allowed the administration to end TPS protections earlier this year.

Billions in Funding and a Hiring Spree

The arrest surge is backed by significant resources. Congress infused ICE with billions of dollars in immigration enforcement funding last summer, enabling the agency to hire 12,000 new deportation officers and investigative agents.

Patricia Quiñonez, a journalist at Utahlozanos covering the Venezuelan immigrant community in Utah, said traffic stop arrests have increased sharply. "They stop you for whatever reason — for example, you don't have a driver's license, your vehicle tags are expired, your windows are more tinted than what is allowed," she told the AP. "From there, they take advantage of the situation and ask about immigration."

People with valid work permits and pending asylum claims are among those arrested, according to Quiñonez, who believes immigrants are being racially profiled during stops.

What It Means for Immigrant Communities

Before Trump took office, monthly arrest figures hovered around 8,000, largely consisting of immigrants transferred from city or state jails. The nearly sixfold increase to July's numbers reflects a fundamental expansion of who ICE targets and how. For Indian and South Asian communities, many of whom hold work visas, pending asylum claims, or TPS designations, the broadened enforcement scope means routine interactions with law enforcement now carry heightened immigration risk.

The data arrives as ICE officers have also started making arrests at scheduled immigration check-ins — appointments that immigrants were previously told to attend as a condition of their cases. Advocates say this practice undermines trust in the legal process and discourages compliance.
